speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, May 6, consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Maclnnis.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on the splendid budget which he presented to the house on May 1. With the exception of a few discordant views- always emanating from the same quarters- this budget has been highly welcomed throughout the country, and I feel certain that the resolutions which will be approved shortly will contribute to the improvement of our economic solution.
Bill No. 19, introduced in the house by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and passed on April 22 last, is an Act to relieve unemployment, promote agricultural settlement, and assist in the conservation and development of our natural and other
resources. The section of the country which I represent is so closely interested in these important problems that I would be remiss to my duty were I not to indicate here the means whereby this country could benefit from the development of the various natural resources to be found in Abitibi.
I approve this government's policy of undertaking and getting undertaken public works that do not involve too heavy an expenditure for the state, in order to provide work for our people and thus do away, as much as possible, with direct relief, while improving the financial situation of the country. Many unemployed desire work that will permit them to live decently and provide for the future, thus setting a good example to the growing generation, instead of continuing to receive the dole which has developed into national exploitation, as may be readily seen in a number of localities.
I have pleasure, sir, in pointing out a few of the national resources of the Abitibi district, the development of which, I am sure, would alleviate unemployment, which threatens our country with disaster. In the vast territory comprised in the Abitib' district numerous gold mines are being worked and many others will be developed in the near future. Besides the mining industry, agriculture offers great possibilities, as well as the lumber industry, which enjoys an excellent local market for its products. There are splendid water powers which, when developed, will supply electric energy for which there will also be a ready market as this form of energy will soon become indispensable.
I shall speak first of the gold mines of my Northern Quebec constituency. Ten years ago they were absolutely unknown. Noranda Mines Limited, scarcely ten years in operation, already have an annual output of over $14,000,000, give employment to more than
2,000	men and provide a livelihood to a population of 16,000. In the same locality, a number of similar industries will soon be in operation, doubling the town's population, increasing the number of men at work and relieving unemployment.
To the northeast, in the same mining area, nine other gold producing mines have started operations in the course of the last six years. They are: Beatty Gold Mines Ltd, O'Brien Gold Mines, Ltd,, Canadian Malartic Gold Mines Ltd, Siscoe Gold Mines Ltd, Shawkey Gold Mining Ltd, Sullivan Gold Mines Ltd, Greene Stabell Gold Mines Ltd, Lamaque Gold Mines Ltd, and Perron Gold Mines Ltd. All these enterprises are very promising; although only at their first stage of development, they may be expected in the neai
The Budget-Mr. Blais

future, to double, even quadruple their output. At the present time, these mines employ-more than 5,000 men, and have become the mainstay of the farming population of this section and provide an additional market for the products of the lumber industry, the yearly output of sawmills being over 36,000,000 feet of lumber, used in the mines and for building purposes in villages and towns. These industries provide part of the livelihood of a population of 40,000.
I do not think that I am too optimistic or far from the truth when I state that by the end of 1936, at least three other gold mines in that section of the country, will get on a production basis, and gradually increase their output as the years go by, thereby increasing the number of workers and reducing unemployment.
The mining bureau at Amos, which is a branch office of the Quebec Department of Mines, gave me, on the 1st of February last, the following data. There are at present twenty-five mining undertakings showing satisfactory progress to date and likely to produce gold in the near future, that is, as soon as good roads for the transportation of their machinery and other material can be built in the district. I shall refer in a moment to the question of good roads, as they constitute, to my mind, the principal means of obtaining satisfactory results.
Furthermore, 125 claim holders employ at present more than 500 men, and their outlook seems most encouraging. As a sequel to these operations we may expect many industries to be established.
The section of Abitibi comprised in Quebec covers an area of 10,000 square miles. Its natural resources are beyond estimation. This region comprises 3,500,000 acres of good farming land on which 35,000 families could be settled. May I add that this district 'holds a splendid future for the farming class, since, at present, we must import nine-tenths of the farm products required by the mining population. Three carloads of provisions are shipped weekly to Amos alone, yet it would be possible to raise these in our district if agriculture were given more encouragement.
The most practical way to carry out a program of development would be, first, to build a good road from Amos to the district of Chibougamau, then to extend it as far as James Bay with crossroads as the development of the country required. Many of the mining properties at Chibougamau are in the hands of reliable capitalists who have long been asking for a suitable highway for the transportation of the material and machinery required to erect plants.

The	distance between Amos	and Chibougameau is about 154 miles, and many promising mineral prospects are to be found along this projected road which would be a factor in developing this large territory for colonization and farming. It would also be necessary to build 15 miles of road from the Sigma	Gold	mines to	Ovicourt	so as tofacilitate the transportation of machinery to a number of mining properties the outlook of which, to date, is among the promising of the north country. The carrying out of this project this spring, would employ thousands of workers, to the great benefit of the unemployed, while developing our natural resources. I note, sir, that from 1930 to 1936, $189,000,000 have been distributed in direct relief, running the country into debt to that extent,	while	giving no	value in	return. Ibelieve	that	if, in the	last five	years, the
government had expended part of that amount in the district I represent, for the development of its natural resources, we would have to-day a smaller debt and fewer unemployed.
Although I am now engaged in farming I have for a long time been interested quite extensively in business, and I am familiar with the conditions existing in the Abitibi district. I have been living there for the last twenty-three years and have closely followed its development, being in contact with every mining company and the business men of a number of localities. I have come to the conclusion that the most effective way of developing our natural resources would be to build good roads. I am aware that the construction of roads is a provincial responsibility; however in a special case such as this one, I think the dominion government should take charge, as the matter has become a national one.
May I refer to the Trans-Canada highway which has now almost reached the Quebec boundary; it should be continued to Amos and Senneterre, from which points, two roads, now under construction, lead to Mont-Laurier, Maniwaki, Montreal and Ottawa. I know that my good friend, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), is also eager to see this road, which would be of very great service, continued into the Abitibi district.
Before resuming my seat, may I quote a statement made by the hon. Minister of Mines (Mr. Crerar) on February 14 last, at the banquet of the Mining Institute held at the Windsor hotel, in Montreal. In the next fifteen years, he stated, the future of our country will be found in the development of our mining industry, which is highly prosperous and most profitable, not only for those directly

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
interested in it, but for the whole country. The hon. minister quoted data found in a publication of the Department of Mines, dated February 14, 1936, and which show that this industry can compare favourably with any other Canadian industry. He added that the small mining district of Cobalt, Sudbury, Porcupine and Kirkland Lake had produced various minerals to an amount exceeding $1,500,000,000, What can we not expect then from our immense district which enjoys the bright prospects I have just shown? The hon. Minister of Mines also referred to the mines of Northern Quebec which, though only at their initial stage of development are on a production basis: Noranda, for example, with an annual output of $14,000,000; Siscoe, which, since its inception has produced approximately $9,000,000; one might also mention the Beatty Gold mines, the O'Brien, Malartic, Lamaque, Sullivan, Green Stabell mines, Bill gold-producing properties still in their primary stage and which will become important mines at an early date.
I wish to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance for having exempted from the income tax imposed on companies all metalliferous mines becoming producers before 1940. These exemptions will cover the first three years of production. This is a strong encouragement to financiers interested in the development of these natural resources.
I cordially invite all the members of this house, but especially the hon. ministers to pay us a visit, in order to see for themselves the great prospects existing in our district.
What I have suggested is quite feasable and we should immediately set to work in our country's interest so as to provide employment for a large number of people and thus conform to the Divine command: Thou shalt earn thy bread by toiling and not by exploiting the toiler. I have set forth a few suggestions in good faith, in the interest of this country, trusting that they may be seriously considered by the house and even put into practice.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While it is my intention to criticize, I hope in a constructive manner, some of the points advanced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in his speech, I want to compliment him upon the arresting tabulation of facts which he presented in relation to the economic situation of this country as he sees it, and I also want to compliment him upon the evident sincerity of his remarks as well as the non-partisan way in which they were delivered.
I propose to confine most of my observations to the speech made by the Minister
of Finance. If I have any time left I shall refer for a moment or two to the speech made yesterday afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis).
At page 2362 of Hansard the Minister of Finance referred to the increase in the physical volume of business in this country, and he very clearly pointed out that from a low point of 67 in 1933 there had been a gradual increase in business to 79-7 in 1934, 94-2 in 1935, 102'4 in 1935-36, and the present economic index, he stated, is at 103-3. Then he.added this significant sentence:
The increases are impressive, particularly when one recalls that this index measures the physical volume of output in nearly all our leading industries as well as freight traffic on our railways, building activity and domestic trade.
That was a generous statement for the Minister of Finance to make, and in my humble opinion it was a remarkable tribute to the business ability and foresight of the former prime minister and his government. A little further on the minister referred to manufacturing, and particularly to the iron and steel industry, with which I was long associated, and he used these words:
In the latter half of 1935, this industry showed striking advances, steel output increasing 23 per cent and pig iron 48 per cent over 1934-
Here again was a tribute to what was done by the previous government in connection with the production of steel in this country. When the late government came into power I believe Canada protected steel plates up to 40 inches in width, but not over that. The late government, rising to the occasion, increased the width to 66 inches, and the steel makers themselves went one step further and rolled steel up to 78 inches in width and an inch and more in thickness. During the last three or four years steel plate production in this country over 40 inches in width, and largely over 66 inches, has been what has kept t'he steel makers in the city of Hamilton busier than they have been for many years in the wider sizes. So I hope that when the revision of the British trade treaties, to which the minister referred, comes up later, he will jealously guard the interests of the steel makers of this country and not lower their protection, under any consideration, below what it is now. On the contrary, if possible I hope he will protect plates up to a width of 78 inches, which they are now rolling. In my humble opinion the late government deserves unstinted praise for what it did in connection with steel, and the minister was generous in refering to this subject.
The Budget-Mr. MacNicol

Further down the page the minister used these significant words in connection with construction:
The construction industry, while still operating on abnormally low levels, enjoyed substantial percentage gains in 1935 over 1934, and the present outlook for building appears to be the best in several years.
I want to pause for a moment or two in connection with construction, for I believe this provides a splendid opportunity for the government now in power to provide thousands' of men with work. The minister is correct when he says construction is increasing; for last year the returns from fifty-eight cities of Canada showed construction in this country at the level of 148,000,000 as compared with $27,000,000 in 1934. All constructive work, such as roads, bridges and so on, rose to the total of $160,000,000 in 1935. That is why I said at the outset that the minister was generous in his statements, which were non-partisan. In tabulating our economic gains he 'has paid a well deserved tribute to the former prime minister and his government, and the result of the policies of the late government in t'heir endeavour to advance prosperity all along the line in this country.
Some days ago I read an article dealing with construction in England, which sets out the remarkable progress that has been made in that country, which is one of the reasons why to-day England is leading the nations of the world in providing employment. When the armistice was signed there were eight million homes in England. As a result of their construction policy in England to-day there are 10,804,888 homes. This has given employment not only to a great number of artisans but also to a large number of factory workers in connection with the necessary material that enters into construction. In addition large orders have been placed in Canada for British Columbia, maritime, Ontario and Quebec lumber. It has been said in the house many times since the beginning of the session that this country should get on with construction. I have endorsed that statement before; I am going to endorse it again. Many of our towns and cities have slums, and if it is at all possible those slums should be removed and adequate homes provided instead. Just how the minister is going to get the money I do not know, but during the last four or five years the federal government has put up $400,000,000 for relief and has voted many millions for the rehabilitation of the western provinces. And rightly so; I am one of those who will support anything reasonable that will make condi-
'Mr. MacNicol.]
tions 'better in the west. I believe the minister can find the money in some way.
The late government was one of the first advocates, I believe, of lowering the gold content of our dollar to 25 cents. I know that up at Milton, Ontario, there is a very able man, Mr. Peter Robertson, to whom the late Mr. George Nicholson, who formerly sat for the constituency represented by the last speaker (Mr. Blais), referred in a very excellent speech in this house a few years ago. Mr. Robertson has some excellent ideas on gold. He wrote a book on the subject which was translated into several languages, at his own expense. This book was sent all over the world and bad a good deal to do with the lowering of the gold coverage behind our dollar.
There may be some other w-ay of getting money with which to proceed with construction, but it should be found in some way because in Canada we 'have 240,000 men who in normal times are employed in the construction industry, but thousands of whom are now unemployed. Taking as a basis the figures as to the amount of labour given per thousand dollars of expenditure in connection with the government building now under construction in Winnipeg, which will cost a million dollars or more, it would take something over $200,000,000 to put at work again the 240,000 men who should be engaged in the construction business but who for the most part are idle. In any event, sir, something must be done to provide more employment.
An. hon. MEMBER:	Social credit.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, not social credit;
I am not in favour of that at all. I have confidence in the ability of the minister to find some sound way of providing money that can be used for proper government support. According to the spring number of Building in Canada construction magazine, taking 1929 as normal, 100. which is different from the usual computation, in 1933, our low point, construction activities stood at 9-2 and by 1935 had risen to 19-7 That is a fairly healthy advance over 1933, and if we continue to advance with increased speed the construction business of this country will soon be back on its feet. But in Great Britain it has got back to 152-5.
I said a moment ago that all works such as roads, and so forth, should be counted in the program to provide work. As we go about this country over our fine concrete roads we frequently come to a narrow bridge. I have in mind two of them on the Dundas road from Toronto to Hamilton, on which

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
road fifty miles an hour is about the usual speed. But when the motorist arrives at the bridge west of Oakville and the bridge at the next river he finds himself in a regular bottle neck. Numerous accidents have occurred there, because the roadway is reduced from about thirty feet to about sixteen feet. In industry manufacturers are compelled to safeguard their employees with all sorts of appliances to keep them from getting hurt in operating or working with the machinery. But the government, responsible for the roads, is causing more deaths by these narrow bridges than industry is causing, and if the provincial government will not act it is high time the federal government did. It could thus give employment to a large number of men.
On page 2366 of Hansard there is a statement made by the minister with which I have to disagree. I quote:
The fruits of economic nationalism in reduced business activity, shrinking governmental revenues and widespread unemployment are such as to justify in abundant measure the efforts which the present government has made, and will continue to make, to free the channels of international trade and expand the markets for our primary and other industries which must otherwise suffer stagnation and drastic readjustment.
The policy of the late government certainly was not economic nationalism, judged from the results it gave, results which the minister himself so highly praised in the quotations I gave a few moments ago.
I would point out further that one of the results of the policy of the late government was, according to Industrial Expansion in Canada, that from August 15, 1930, to the same date in 1935, 272 branch factories came into this country from the United States, Great Britain and other countries. These 272 factories make automotive parts, electrical parts, foodstuffs, machinery, metal products, chemicals, drugs, wood products, textiles and leather, etc. That is a very substantial amount of new business brought into this country by the activities of the late government. If the present minister and his government can do as well in the next five years they will be doing very nicely indeed.
I have a clear recollection of the last time this same policy, lower and lower tariffs, was introduced in this country, and I hope the same disasters will not result that accrued between 1922 and 1926. On several occasions I had to attend employment conferences of one kind or another, and I know that in September, 1924-the present Minister oi Finance was not then a member of the government, but the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was in the house then and he will remember-there were deputations from all
over the country protesting against the free trade policy of the government of that day. There were protests from boards of education, city councils, township councils, county councils, labour organizations and every kind of organization in the country. In September, 1924, a delegation came to Ottawa and presented figures to the government indicating the contraction in business and manufacturing. Taking into account new industries started the net contraction was as follows, as a direct result, I believe, of the trade policy of the government of the day:

A new plant in this country means a great deal in addition to the direct employment it gives. There is a new can factory going up- I believe it is practically in operation now- in West York. The minister referred to it some time ago, but his facts were inaccurate as I understood him, if he said' that the trade treaties had something to do with its coming here. The trade treaties had no more to do with it than the man in the moon, because the arrangements were made last September; in fact the original designs were prepared some three or four years ago, after the Campbell Soup company itself came to this country. The new can factory to which I refer is about the same size as the Campbell Soup factory, and if it takes the same amount of material as the Campbell plant it will require some seven or eight hundred carloads of material of all kinds, such as sand, gravel, brick, piping, glass, paint, roofing and machinery, etc. So that every new factory started in this country means business not only for the men erecting it but for the factories supplying the building material. I hope the proposals of the government will not result in the lessening of factory building.
A day or two ago I read in a publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce of May 2 something which shows that all is not gold that glitters. To me the budget is nothing more or less than a big guess. Municipalities and business corporations are compelled to keep their expenditures within their revenues. If they do not, and I am talking particularly of municipalities, they are not only severely criticized; they are taken to task by the provincial governments. I never could understand why there should be one set of rules for municipalities and a different set of rules for the provinces and the dominion, but apparently such is the case, for with the latter unbalanced budgets are the rule rather than the exception. In my humble judgment the dominion budget should have been balanced this year. It is safe to assume, I think, that any government that does not take drastic measures to balance its budget within the first year will find it increasingly difficult to do so as its term of office gradually draws to a close.
There is a fast growing conviction that the great Liberal party is not fulfilling the pledges it made to the Canadian people, through the Prime Minister, on the evening of October 14. Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon the very clear and excellent exposition he gave to the house on Friday afternoon. I think those of us who were privileged to listen to him on that occasion realized that he had an unsurpassed grasp of the problems confronting the country. I should like to commend him also for some things I find in the budget. To those of us who come from western Canada and who represent rural constituencies the tariff reductions are indeed well received. I have particular reference to the reduction in the duty on gasoline, and to something which I think must have escaped the scrutiny of most hon. members, the comparatively large reduction in the duty on dis-

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
tillate, which, as we all know, is of primary importance to the producers who use that form of fuel for the operation of their tractors in the agricultural sections of Canada.
I am also glad that the duty on agricultural implements has been reduced to 7J per cent, but after listening to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) a short time ago I wonder why the duty has not been wiped out altogether. If agricultural implements are purchased in the town of Halloek, Minnesota, at higher prices than in the town of Emerson, Manitoba, there is no reason in the world why a protective tariff should be necessary for the Canadian implement industry. May I say to the hon. member for Davenport that those of us who come from western Canada are just as mindful of the interests of the men who work in the implement factories as are any other members of the house. But I should like to point out that an ever increasing percentage of the material and work entering into the production of agricultural and other implements is provided by means of machines, and the human element enters less and less into the production of implements and other commodities. I noted with a great deal of interest and some pleasure that one of these implement companies had set aside pensions for 206 of its work people who had reached the age of sixty-five. But may I point out that in all probability some of the funds for those pensions was provided by farmers who. because of the high prices of implements and for other reasons, lost their equities in their farms and now have no pension except the old age pension to guard them in the future.
The contention is made constantly that the implement companies are losing money, but I am hopeful that the inquiry into the agricultural implement industry which is now going on will demonstrate that at least a part of the losses are due to overcapitalization and overbuilding. Very recently, for example, the British government sent a commission to Canada to investigate the automobile industry in regard to the provisions under which imperial products may enter the British market. I happen to know that this commission refused to include in the overhead of at least one of our great corporations a plant in the city where I live which was not being used, and warehouse space in Walkerville, in this province of Ontario. Overbuilding and overcapitalization will account in no small measure for some of the difficulties of these companies.
We are pleased also to note the reductions, substantial in some respects and small in others, in relation to textiles. That is an industry which for a long time has had not only quite adequate protection but comparatively high protection. And, coming from the west where once in a while the people cross

the border, we are pleased with the provision that we are to have the same privilege that is enjoyed by United States tourists coming into Canada, under which tourists returning to Canada from other countries will be allowed to bring in $100 worth of goods free of duty.
I hope that some day not only the people who are privileged to have automobiles or who can buy steamship tickets, but people who cannot afford these things will be able to bring in one hundred dollars' worth of goods from time to time. But these provisions please me.
There is, however, one thing in the budget which I am exceedingly sorry to see, and that is the increase in the sales tax, which will fall very heavily upon the masses of the people who cannot afford to pay it. In Alberta for example the provincial government has also placed in effect a sales tax of two per cent, so that the people of Alberta will be charged a sales tax of ten per cent, which is exceedingly high. Already the effect of the sales tax can be seen in relation to automobiles; for it has been stated that the price of cars will be raised to the extent of the tax, which will restore the former price that was reduced by the trade treaty with the United States. I had hoped also, having regard to the criticism that was levelled against the sugar tax when it was instituted by the late government, that that tax would be wiped out. It is a tax upon the luxury of the poor. I well remember how a few days after the tax was first instituted I was driving in Saskatchewan with the reeve of a muneipality, who had a large family. He had bought a sack of sugar, paying the increased price of $2 per hundred pounds. He said: "I do not think the government of Canada realize just what that tax means to me." He pointed out that he had to take to the store forty dozen more eggs at five cents a dozen to pay the tax. It is indeed a tax which bears heavily upon the poor, a tax even on the candy used by our children.
Tariff reductions have received a great deal of discussion in this house, but again let me repeat what I and others of our group have said before, that tariff reductions, while useful, will not solve our problems of trade. Why not consider what other nations are actually doing at this time, namely, directing .trade to those who will trade with them? In that connection the policy should be to trade as nearly as possible to the same extent with those who trade with us. Of course that involves controlled exports and imports, something which perhaps the present government is not prepared even to consider, and for which public opinion and public support will have to be moulded as the days

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
go by. Our sister dominion, New Zealand, is, I believe, taking control of the milling and wheat industry of that country from the first of May. Of course it is not comparable with the same industry in Canada, for in New Zealand wheat production is quite a secondary industry. But on August 1 of this year the government of New Zealand will also take control of all dairy produce, will export it and set its domestic price through a single governmental agency, guaranteeing to the farmer a fair return and selling the product abroad with the government's stamp upon it. That industry is comparable with our wheat industry because it is the primary industry of New Zealand. Switzerland demands direct trading relationships; Germany, Sweden and to a degree France, Italy and some other countries are demanding a quid pro quo in commerce with foreign nations. The world trading relationships are moving in that direction. Russia under a different plan and perhaps for a different purpose has been conducting her externa! trade along much the same lines for a considerable time.
Canada, we are told, faces grave problems. One hon. member has said that unemployment is our greatest problem; another says the railway problem is the most serious. But transcending both in my opinion is the problem of agriculture. In his speech the minister recognized its gravity. But I submit that other than the items to which I specifically referred there is little further hope in the budget for the agricultural producer. One thing that worries me at the moment, in connection with the reports we are getting from western Canada of weather and soil conditions there at the present time, is; What will happen if this year western Canada produces a bumper crop? What allotment of money have the government made to cope with the situation that may conceivably arise? What plans have the government for financing the situation which may come about this autumn? Drought, grasshoppers and rust have relieved us of the necessity of facing that problem in the last two or three years. This year, although the carry-over will be reduced, it will still be large. We congratulate ourselves that during the past year we were able to find a market in the United States for some of our farm produce. But speaking at Lincoln, Nebraska, last Monday evening in the state university, the Secretary of Agriculture, Mr. Wallace, said:
The main fact to bear in mind, however, is that these increased imports were due to an absolutely unprecedented situation. I suppose the same situation is not likely to occur in the same degree for another one hundred years, unless our climate is changing drastically.
There is simply no point in viewing the farm imports of 1935, which were caused by the drought of 1934, as reflecting a normal situation facing the American farmer.
Our recent trade treaty with the United States will not help us in relation to that problem. In the same speech Mr. Wallace went on to say;
One might go on to show the extremely small size of farm imports, even in the face of the terrible drought of 1934, as compared with our normal production. It is truly surprising that quite the worst drought since the Civil War should result in imports of corn representing only about two per cent of our average production; wheat a little over three per cent, beef, including canned beef, three per cent of average slaughter; pork one-tenth of one per cent of average production; and butter one per cent.
Even under drought conditions the American union imported relatively little, and once good conditions return they can probably satisfy their own market to the full. Not only that, but Secretary Wallace indicated that under such conditions he hoped they would be able once again to enter upon the export of agricultural goods. In the same speech he said:
As supplies of wheat and pork and other export products increase with normal weather, we should regain a part of our foreign trade in these products, too.
So that not only are we faced with a loss of the market we had to the south, but we are faced with competition in the world market from surplus products of farms in the United States. This year those United States farms may become a real factor in the world agricultural situation, and should Russia also go on the expor market the situation would be considerably aggravated. Of course, as was shown yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), fortunately for Canada farms, Russia has a rising standard of life, and as the standard rises consumption increases; consequently the danger of competition from Russia decreases proportionately. But we cannot lose sight of the fact that Russian agricultural sowings of grain in this year are higher than in preceding years, and with improved methods and a scientific background we do not know what the future has in store for us so far as competition with Russia is concerned.
And so I say: Will not the government realize that old-fashioned or "normal" trade, as it is called, is done? Our producers need blankets, boots, clothing, cutlery and a multitude of other things. One has but to travel and visit the homes of the producers to find that what I have said is abundantly evident, [n Great Britain and other European countires there are people who are unemployed
The Budget-Mr. Coldweli

and who could make these goods. They are underfed because they are unemployed. France, Germany, Great Britain aad other countries need wheat, beef, butter, pork, fruit and so on. "Oh," some one says, "if we attempted to exchange their commodities for ours we would close our factories." Well, gentlemen, the factories are closed now. It is true that we face a dilemma; I realize it. We face that dilemma because of the unplanned and unintelligent economic system to which we hare bound our faith. Sooner or later we shall have to make a choice, and to my mind the choice will be between the encouragement of native, natural industries in Canada and the continued encouragement of tariff-nurtured ventures which are monopolistic and powerful and have sheltered themselves behind tariff barriers of various kinds.
I heard the leader of the opposition use the word "parasitic" in one of his radio addresses, but perhaps in another connection. I use the same word when I say that these parasitic industries, if I may so describe them, are destroying the basic industries upon which they feed. We must face that fact. Much of the soil drifting and soil depletion in western Canada is due to that same kind of economic structure. Again may I quote from the same speech by Secretary Wallace:
Farmers know that the reasons for ruthless exploitation of soil have often been economic- that under pressure of extreme supply and price fluctuations they have been alternately forced by ruinously low returns and induced by boom conditions to mine and sell soil fertility, or to expand the farm plant by turning under millions of acres of grass lands which should have remained in sod. I believe that farmers understand the public and private importance of stabilizing production, stabilizing prices, and of maintaining the productivity of farm land for years to come.
If that is true of the United States it is equally true of Canada. What hope do we find in the budget of stabilizing agricultural conditions in this dominion? Unplanned production with unplanned markets are bringing Canada, in common with may other parts of the world, to the very brink of economic and social chaos; for reduced purchasing power on the farms and in industry reduces consumption. By rational control and by trade exchanges abroad we must increase purchasing power and consumption in Canada. Of course that is a tremendous undertaking, and I do not envy the task of a finance minister who has to cope with it, but I submit that it is not an impossible task.
What preparations are being made by the government, the Minister of Finance and the Bank of Canada to meet the possibility of financial chaos in the near future? When we pick up our daily papers we read disturb-

ing accounts of the financial activities of almost every country in the world-the United States, France, Germany, Italy, of course, and even Great Britain. What preparations are we making to meet the situation which will develop? Are we going to follow the United States in the inflation which at the moment looks almost inevitable? If so, to what extent and how will that affect our trade relationship with our best customer, Great Britain? Conceivably it may assist us for a time, if we follow the American dollar. On the other hand, unless we are prepared to meet the situation, the ultimate dislocation may have disastrous results. Of course this involves a discussion of banking and finance. I do not purpose discussing those matters this afternoon, except in so far as they relate to the budget proposals.
It seems to me the time has come when national ownership of our central bank, our currency and our credit, and their use for national ends, is tremendously important. Before parliament prorogues we should give these matters full consideration.
The minister aims at something more nearly approaching a balanced budget. In the course of observations I made on a previous occasion I said I was not particularly interested in balancing the budget, but that I was more interested in the balancing of human welfare. That is still my opinion. The minister admits that there may be hon. members who will criticize the budget as a move in the direction of further deflation. I should like to hear the hon. members for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) and Rosthern (Mr. Tucker)-the latter is in his seat-comment on that particular opinion expressed by the minister.
In that connection I should like to place on Hansard a quotation as it appears in a publication known as Index, No. 123, of March, 1936, published by the Swedish central bank, and which is an authoritative document on the Swedish financial system. Professor Bertil Ohlin, referring to the improvement in Sweden, has this to say:
This change of circumstances is all the more remarkable if _ we compare them with conditions in a typical gold parity country such as France. As part of their deflationary policy the governments there, in order to wipe out the deficit on the budget, have effected one reduction in expenditure after another, yet they have found, much to their chagrin, that the revenue has declined as speedily as the expenditure and that there is still a huge deficit. This actually applies also to the budget for 1936. Formally it is balanced, it is true, but the equilibrium has been achieved by the transfer of heavy non-profitable expenditure, e.g. considerable defence items, to a special budget. It cannot be said therefore that the budget is effectively balanced.
This course of development leads us to a very important conclusion regarding financial

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
policy in periods of severe and prolonged depression. The fa!ling-off in government revenues caused thereby and the increase in expenditure that is generally called for, e.g. for combatting unemployment, are so heavy that neither economies nor higher tax rates effected on a scale that is practically feasible can fully compensate for them. In other words, it is not possible to balance a budget so long as a policy of deflation is pursued.
Recent events in a number of countries show, on the other hand, that as soon as the deflation ceases and economic conditions improve the equilibrium in the state finances is restored. Government revenues rise and expenditure on unemployment goes down. It is really something of a paradox that in a country such as Sweden, where no attempt was made during the crisis to arrive at a balance, the budget is nevertheless now balanced, whereas a lack of equilibrium in the state finances has pre-sisted in France, where the governments have made the balancing of the budget the primary object of policy.
It seems to me that that is an opinion worthy of study. In some degree it is the same contention which we in this little group have made so often. The balancing of a budget curtails consumption and to that degree makes economic improvement more difficult. Whilst I mention what Sweden had done in this regard, I am not forgetful of what it has done in the utilization of some of the great monopolies to assist in the financing of social services. Sweden is considering the utilization of further monopolies for this purpose. I commend this suggestion to the government and the minister, not for inclusion in this budget, as that is manifestly impossible now, but for consideration as a means of improving our economic position sometime during the next two or three years, when I fancy the minister will be faced with a financial situation even graver than that facing him to-day.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maolnnis), in which I concur, advocates a levy on accumulated wealth to reduce the burden of our national debt. I believe this must come. Increased taxation of incomes in the higher brackets will undoubtedly have to come. In this regard may I say I have been told on quite good authority that there are men with comparatively large fortunes made in this country who have transferred their domiciles from one province to another in order to escape death duties or to obtain a reduction in such levies. I heard of one gentleman who has removed himself to the Bahama islands, I believe it is, and obtained domicile in order to escape taxation upon his fortune by the country in which he made it. That is not patriotism, and it is an action which should be prevented by the parliament of Canada. Such things should be treated as criminal offences.

Not only have we to
consider the public debt of Canada, but we have to consider the tremendous private debt. Of course the budget does not deal with this particular form of debt except in some minor details. At this point I should like to say that I am rather disturbed at the tremendous burden of debt upon people who have produced, who have worked in an endeavour to obtain a competence in the country in which
The Budget-Mr. ColdweU.

they live, and who now find that under present economic conditions the things for which they worked are passing from them. I was sorry to learn from some farmers in my constituency that they had been informed that the payments made in relation to the 1930 certificates were no longer under their control. In many instances they had hypothecated them because of financial obligations and to-day they find themselves in no better position on account of these payments, except for the reduction of their debt, than they were in before. When the matter was before the house I was under the impression that the payments would be made only to the person who owned the certificate and who had delivered the wheat to the country elevator.
I see that my time has just about expired, and in closing I would say this. This house and the country as well will be faced with a tremendous problem in the next two or three years. Every constructive thought should be brought to bear upon the problem that confronts us, and we should not frown upon ideas because they are new, no matter from what quarter they may come. If we study the solutions that have been arrived at elsewhere and examine suggestions that are put forward here and in other places from time to time, I am quite convinced that we shall pass through the difficulties that we face to-day to a better and a fairer social order.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to speak in French, with which I am more familiar and which is my mother tongue. I am well aware of the courtesy of hon. members and I am sure that the house will extend to me the same hospitality that is shown by the old French legislature in Quebec when once m a while a member speaks in English. I am proud of the spirit of fraternity displayed by the different races composing this assembly.
Before continuing my remarks in French I wish to say this to the Minister of Marine (Mr. Howe). A speaker of the unionist party in Quebec, who happens to be the local member for Portneuf, said the other day on the radio that the political spirit and fanaticism had induced federal Liberal members representing the different counties in Quebec to leave the portfolio of Marine in the hands of an Ontario member. I simply say that this local unionist member was talking through his hat, and though a pilot and a director of the Montreal Pilots' Association, he was certainly not speaking on behalf of that body. The permanent members of the Montreal pilots' organization had an opportunity to confer with the Minister of Marine and they were absolutely satisfied with the interview and the interest which the hon. gentleman showed in

receiving them. This organization has always fought for its rights and has never acted in that way before towards the marine and pilotage authorities. It is true the minister is from Ontario, but we see beyond the limits of our own province and we believe that Ontario is a part of Canada just as much as is Quebec. The pilots know that the minister is a Canadian through and through and is doing splendid work, and this isolated attack will not stop him from devoting himself to maritime interests on the St. Lawrence and elsewhere in Canada.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to continue in French the few observations I have to offer.
In spite of the eight years I have spent in the Quebec legislature, it is not without emotion that I rise to address a gathering composed of so many of Canada's most eminent public men. I would not wish any utterance of mine to hurt anyone's feelings. A soldier of the valiant Liberal army, I cherish but one wish: to bring to the discussions of the house the expression of my ideas, believing them to be worthy of utterance before the representatives of the nation, and I have but one thought, a thought which, I believe, should fill the mind of every good patriot

that of contributing, in the measure of my capacity, to the welfare and advancement of our glorious country, the finest in the world.
I do not wish to continue, Mr. Speaker, before tendering to you my most sincere congratulations on your elevation to the speakership of the house. The glorious exception whose voice was raised in objection to 3'our nomination as First Commoner of the land only served to confirm the general sentiment. Your personal qualities and your deep knowledge of parliamentary procedure give you an indisputable right to your high office. Your manner of conducting the proceedings of the house has established your worthiness to occupy it.
May I be allowed to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on his clear and frank statement of the financial and economic situation of the country. The Minister of Finance has confidence in the future of Canada and of the Canadian people. He said the other day-and all Canadians should ponder his words-that we must have confidence and that we must preach that confidence without which the nation cannot advance and which is the antithesis of all ideas based on the interests of groups, of cities or of provinces.
To seek to enlist popular support for a theory by holding before the people prospects of ease to be obtained at the cost of

The Budget-Mr. Gauthier
a minimum of effort; to group forces sometimes produced by entirely different energies, in order to ensure the momentary success of a party; to preach a theory the application of which would load on the shoulders of the state all the charges of the country; to make the government the controller of all the activities of the people; to create a sort of national bureaucracy by restraining the hand of the individual; to establish in the nation a system of extreme paternalism; to try to divide a country by calling up questions of rights disregarded and of differences of interests; in short, to create a small state within the larger one, those are some of the ideas-I have certainly not enumerated them all-that are current in the world and in this country to-day, and whose progress we should not fail to watch.
I said a moment ago that I was a soldier of the Liberal army; I may add that I am proud of it and that I have no hesitation in following the lead of my chiefs. Let us open the pages of our political history; let us read the ones that the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier wrote from 1896 to 1911; let us recall the economic situation as it was under his successor the right honourable the present prime minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and let us compare that period with the years of Conservative rule. On the one hand, we find Canada enjoying a flourishing trade and profitable international relations, the efforts of Liberal governments being always directed to the same end: lowering of taxation and reduction of the debt by the exercise of rigid economy. Under Conservative governments, on the other hand, we find our debt ever increasing, our trade strangled by excessive tariffs and the people increasingly burdened by the weight of taxation. A good Canadian summarized the situation very clearly in saying:	"Conservative governments pile up debts and Liberal governments pay them off."
I do not wish to be too hard on those who have nearly all disappeared1-the Canadian people having made sure that they obtained a well-deserved rest.-but I cannot help remembering the election of 1930, with its butter in the province of Quebec, the numerous conferences that were to raise Canada from its ashes, the manner in which the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was attacked for advocating the repeal of Section 98, and the famous posters, as grotesque as they were insulting. I will refrain from mentioning Mr. Sage's course of economics and apologetics.
In 1930 the people decided to try an experiment. In 1935 they thought better of it. And that government, that cost the people
the large sum of 800 millions of dollars, is still deploring the fragility of things human and wondering at the good sense of the voters.
We, also, hear the cries of the mothers, but we heed them. Instead of treating the symptoms, as inexpert physicians do, the government attacks the disease at its root. Our trade, freed from its bonds, is back into its normal course, and the Canadian people find opening up before them, in consequence of the reciprocity (agreement, a market of 100 millions consumers. The late government had understood at last, but too late. The tories tried, in 1935, to make an issue of their efforts to negotiate the famous treaty that they had killed with the aid of the nationalists of 1911. Their repentance was tardy, but their contrition did not seem to be perfect-them came their penance.
The Liberal party must now reconstruct. As all sound builders, they must start at the foundation. The edifice cannot possibly rise in a night. Being a skilled architect, the Prime Minister of this country has surrounded himself with able men. They are only too ready to place their knowledge at his disposal and, judging from the numerous testimonials which are unceasingly pouring in since the Minister of Finance presented his splendid budget, the Canadian people have regained confidence and hope to live again years of prosperity and peace.
I stated just now that the economic structure of this country cannot be built up in a night; there will be delays and setbacks. Among these will be found unemployment. Many are astonished to hear it still spoken of; it was to have been solved so rapidly! Unfortunately the problem is still with us. I recognize with many others that strenuous efforts were made to alleviate unemployment. Public works, colonization, etc., are so many remedies used to relieve it. Public works are a palliative, a treatment of symptoms; no sooner are they completed than the unemployed reappear as numerous as ever, waiting for further works to start. But governments must find revenues to meet all these expenditures.
The freedom and development of trade, tested remedies resorted to by a Liberal administration, will soon relieve this constraint, anxiety and fear experienced by the victims of an unrelenting congestion. Like individuals, society must breathe, financial organizations must consolidate and expand, trade must be encouraged and mutual trust must revive between nations as well as between individuals. For twenty years, high tariff barriers have prepared the crisis from which we have so long suffered. Let us hope that the same blunder will never reoccur and that the
The Budget-Mr. Gauthier

general interests of countries will displace selfish personal interests, be they those of the financiers, "corporatists" theorists, politicians or individuals.
The Canadian nation owes its birth and development to the loyalty and self-sacrifice of its citizens. It cannot continue if self interest is to prevail. Inhabiting the same country, belonging to different races and creeds, having interests often diametrically opposed to each other, we must even bring a strictly national viewpoint to the solution of the problems with which we are faced. Away with interprovincial boundaries and with racial distrust! Loyal subjects of one king, governed by federal or provincial laws of one country, all Canadians, be they French, English, Scotch, Irish, living in the west or in the maritime provinces, should feel that they are brothers of those belonging to the same races living in 'the central provinces. To each one his rights, his creed, his language and his aspirations! The confederation of the Canadian provinces has survived to this day and it behooves us all to strengthen it, if possible, and cause other countries to envy the harmony that reigns here. May I recall the old but always true saying, dear to my colleague from Quebec South-west (Mr. Parent) "United we stand, divided we fall."
I referred, sir, to the means of relieving unemployment; I mentioned colonization. I reside in a province which has understood the necessity of directing its activities towards that goal; an extensive program of settlement has been carefully prepared by the Quebec government and is now being carried out. Thousands of settlers coming from the cities, many of whom are farmers' sons and urban workers, have been settled on lands chosen by agents or colonization missionaries. New centres appear here and there: Afeitibi, Temiskaming, Gaspe, Temiscouata and others which will open up new avenues to trade and industry, to the worker and even to the professional man, thereby relieving the overflow of our cities by directing it elsewhere. Is this not, sir, a true remedy, is this not attacking the root of the evil, that is the disproportion existing between urban and rural populations? I believe so, and the highest church and civil authorities have realized it long before I did. The movement Should spread to the whole country, in spite of adverse criticism and of opposition from whatever source.
Our fertile lands are great in extent and only require to be stirred to produce. Many of our natural resources still lie idle and only await the appearance of the hardy toiler. Why not have recourse to the strong arms of Canadian citizens?

Canadians are still willing to work and if we direct them well, if we place at their service the means at our disposal, if we furnish their initiative with the opportunity to manifest and develop itself, there will be no need, in order to revive their confidence, to preach so many doctrines, sometimes brilliant but too often deceptive, because of their false conception of the relation between the state, whose duty it is to govern wisely, and the citizen.
The state helps its citizens to live; it cannot undertake to provide a living for everybody. The state, by its laws, encourages and facilitates work. It is not a fountain of plenty in which all may dip without accomplishing any work. The state works; the people must do likewise. I place too much faith in the Canadian people to doubt of their abounding resourcefulness. The Liberal government recognizes this and its entire program breathes work and reconstruction.
Statistics show that nearly 2,000,000 persons still depend on direct relief. Although industrial employment is on the increase-I think it is the young and brilliant Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) who made that statement the other day-the number of those who depend on direct assistance is not decreasing. The constant increase of the population with its new contingent of industrial workers, the inventions and use of new machines and new processes explain the present situation. May I, sir, mention another explanation. I wish to speak of the important and delicate subject of immigration, and with that I will close my remarks.
I well recall that in 1930 Conservative speakers decried the Liberal party for having permitted immigration. The Conservative government were going to prohibit it entirely. This promise, like the one in connection with butter, was earned away on the winds as easily as are the autumn leaves. The Conservative government did make an effort and, by order in council No. 695 of March 21, 1931, restricted the flow of immigration. On September 6, 1931, another order in council, No. 2115, was passed in connection with Asiatic immigration. And here is the result. To a question I asked in the house, I received a reply that from March, 1930, to March, 1934, 147,660 immigrants entered Canada. Of this number 73,846 came from the British Isles. From April 1, 1934, to January 31, 1936, 21,996 immigrants entered Canada, which must also be added to the figure given in the first reply, making a total of 169,656 immigrants. And immigration had ceased!
I am not called upon to establish a parallel with immigration previous to 1930 or 1911;

The Royal Assent
it was much greater. But at that time we had not, out of a population of 10,000,000 people, 2,000,000 persons depending on direct relief. When the government is making every effort to find and provide work, why should they add a new problem to the existing one?
A few moments ago I asked that new centres be opened to settlement and that the unemployed be put to work at the development of our natural resources. But if immigration does not cease, there will be no end to unemployment. In spite of all that may be said, I cannot believe that it is only capitalists who are entering the country.
No, sir, to my mind our immigration laws should be revised once more and we should tell those who feel an irrestible urge to come to Canada, to wait until we have solved the unemployment problem and have so amended our laws as to greatly restrict the choice of immigrants.
I quite admit that there is room in this country for many more millions of people. I am in favour of admitting people from the British Isles and British born or French citizens! But it is rumoured, as may be seen by articles in a number of Canadian newspapers, that people from other countries cross over to England, become naturalized, and then enter Canada. I do not wish to ostracize any race. All are entitled to a place on this earth. But each nation is also entitled to choose its new citizens. Let those who are obliged to resort to subterfuges to enter Canada remain in their own country. We wish to ascertain where we are at and know something about those who wish to settle here. That is all I have to say for the present on this question. I trust that the government will accept my remarks on immigration in the same spirit as those I uttered a few moments ago.
Still speaking from a national viewpoint, having but one object in mind, the welfare, harmony, prosperity and progress of Canada, I remain true and loyal to my compatriots, to the Liberal principles which are dear to me, and to the Canadian fatherland for which I cherish a great love. It is my intention to keep posted, by every possible means at my disposal, on the human capital that comes to us.
Mr. Speaker I wish to pay homage to my constituents of the beautiful county of Portneuf. I have their interests at heart and I count on their loyal cooperation and frankly Canadian support to carry out my work on their behalf.
May I, sir, direct the attention of the government to a rather important problem interesting the county of Portneuf: that of the production and sale of charcoal. I have already discussed this question in the Quebec
Legislative Assembly and I now ask the federal government to help us find markets for this product of Portneuf county, especially to help us in meeting a ruinous, I may even say an unfair competition. Mr. Speaker, in closing my remarks may I be permitted to express the wish-and in this I feel I have the support of my hon. friends in the far corners of the House-that some day, in order that we might better enjoy the splendid speeches delivered in the house, the government will at the suggestion of His Honour the Speaker, instal microphones with loud speakers in the four comers of the Chamber, thus enabling us, the back-benchers, to hear as well as those more centrally seated.
