subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Maclnnis.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is in his seat, as I desire to extend to him my sincere and hearty congratulations upon the manner in which he presented the budget. The clarity of his language, the thoroughness of the examination of the public accounts and the general manner of presentation were admirable, and I have no hesitation whatever in extending to the minister my earnest congratulations.
Under our democratic system it has long been one of the cherished rights of the people to present their claims to parliament through their chosen representatives, and for an equally long time the occasion of the presentation of the budget by the Minister of Finance has been considered the most opportune moment for a statement of those claims by the people's representatives. Parliament is supposed, in theory at least, to give earnest consideration to those needs or grievances or claims as the case may be.
The budget itself discloses the maximum that the government is prepared to do to relieve the distress or to meet the needs and claims of the people. I shall discuss the present budget from that standpoint. It is my intention to leave the discussion of all detail until the committee stage when there will be opportunity bo discuss and examine the various phases of the budget and the statement made by the minister, so I trust it will not be thought that because I do not in the limited time at my disposal to-night enter into a discussion of any of these matters, this is on account of any lack of appreciation of their importance.
[Mr Speaker.]
The Minister of Finance said, as reported on page 2384 of Hansard:
I am confident that common sense and sound economic policies can solve our immediate problems.
These words suggest to me two questions: first what are our immediate problems, or what were the immediate problems that the minister had in mind as disclosed in his remarks; and second, what does he mean by "sound economics"? As to the problems the minister had in mind, I do not think it is difficult to recognize them. They are: First, the promotion of foreign trade; second, how to balance the budget, and third, the protection of Canada's credit. I do not think he would disagree with me when I say that these seem to me to rank first in importance in his mind. A vital question is: How does the minister apply his principle of 'sound economics' to the solution of these problems? Let us take first the promotion of foreign trade. I will again quote the minister, because it is highly important that we get a clear understanding of his attitude towards the general situation. On page 2366 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
It is not putting it too strongly to say that foreign trade is the very life-blood of Canada.
These are very strong words. Perhaps I should quote a little further from the same part of his speech. He said:
Every step which helps to provide markets for our agriculture brings nearer that day when the Canadian farmer, receiving more for his products than it costs to produce them, will once more provide, through the stimulus of his purchasing power, a sound basis for national prosperity.
I do not take exception to either of these sentences; that is, I do not take particular objection to their form. I object, however, to the assertion, which they seem to me to make, that the whole solution of Canada's problems, agricultural and others, is to be found in the extension of foreign trade. It will not be possible for me to examine that aspect of the question in detail, and I do not intend to go into figures, but I will make one or two observations about it. I prefer the term "external trade" rather than "foreign trade," because the largest proportion of our outside trade is done with the British empire and I do not think we should speak of that as foreign trade. The government seem to rest all their hopes for recovery on the increase of our external trade. I submit to the minister and to the government that they are blindly ignoring imminent domestic problems the solution of which must come from within Canada. I do not care to what extent our foreign trade is increased, there are most

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
imminent problems, to which I shall make reference later, that must find their solution within Canada. But this is the government's only answer to the appeals of those who are suffering. For instance, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has on more than one occasion intimated that the measures which he has introduced for the relief of unemployment are temporary, bridging the gap as it were, until, as he said, our foreign trade restores us to a condition of prosperity. In my own riding of Kootenay East, in and around Fernie, Michel, and Coal Creek, we have a body of miners. Let me tell the minister and the house of the conditions under which these miners have been living for the past six years. A great many of them have not been working at all. Those who have been working, particularly at Coal Creek and Fernie, several hundreds of them, have for six years been getting two or three days' work a week, and no relief, because when they are working two or three days a week they are not allowed to go on relief. These are splendid men, fearless in the hour of danger; they are exactly the type of men who performed heroic service in Nova Scotia the other day. They are good fathers and husbands; most of them have families, and all they are asking is that they be permitted to work. Oh, the minister replies, we have recently arrived at a modus vivendi with Haiti for foreign trade. He says: We have under discussion some arrangements in regard to extending our treaty with France. He says also: We reduced the duty on rabbit skins from Belgium. Are these and other efforts towards the extension of foreign trade an answer to those miners? Is it a common sense answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If I may be permitted to interrupt, my hon. friend is unfair in making that observation. Taking the duty off rabbit skins from Belgium must in its relation to foreign trade be considered in connection with what Belgium took off Canadian imports.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which was a violation of the most favoured nation treaty.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I quite appreciate that, but the minister must have a little sense of humour-well, I should not say humour-to understand the ghastly nature of such an answer, when those miners ask for an opportunity of providing food and clothing for their children, to tell them: Our answer is in the extension of our external trade. What I am seeking to impress upon the minister's mind is this, that in the presentation of this budget and in these matters to which I am now referring there is no answer to the miners of Fernie and, of course, to others in similar circumstances. But I say this: I doubt whether 12739-166
there is in Canada any place where men, women and children have suffered more than have the miners and their families at Fernie.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Due to the absence of foreign trade in their province.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister told us that last year foreign trade increased $151,000,000 over the figure for 1934. That, I think, is very creditable. But in that same year the numbers on relief did not decrease. There was no decrease, but there was a distinct advance in foreign trade. Supposing this year there is an advance of $150,000,000 or $200,000,000; if it has the same effect as it had last year it will not help these people on relief at all. That is the point I am trying to make.
But the minister says, no doubt: See how it helps the farmer. In fact, in my quotation a minute ago from the hon. gentleman's speech he indicated that an extension of foreign trade was the very foundation or basis of national recovery. Well, let us look at that statement briefly. No doubt an extension of foreign trade will help to some extent, but let us bear in mind that about ninety per cent or more of the products of the farm are marketed and consumed in Canada. I have before me a list which I shall not trouble to put on Hansard at present, but with the exception of cheese, wheat and apples, practically every other article produced on the farm is consumed and marketed in Canada to an extent of about ninety-five per cent. So, an extension of foreign trade is not going to help them so much, because world prices are invariably lower than domestic prices, and if there is one thing the farmer needs more than another it is an increase in prices. As the minister himself asserted in his thesis every step which helps to provide markets for agriculture brings nearer that day when the Canadian farmer through the stimulus of his purchasing power will introduce a sound basis for recovery. I have already indicated that the great bulk of these goods are marketed in Canada. External prices are invariably lower than domestic prices. How then can we hope, by an extension of external trade, to make such a recovery in the condition of the farmer, or, as the minister says, to lay a foundation for the recovery of conditions throughout the whole country.
For a moment let us turn to the question of balancing the budget, and here again I quote the minister:
What we can and must do is to make an immediate appreciable approach to a balanced budget.
And then follows what is to me a very strange statement:

The Budget-Mr. Stevens

I feel it necessary to budget for a deficit this fiscal year of something less than $100,000,000.
He is budgeting definitely for a deficit. That is a policy of defeat, and it is disclosing a stubborn adherence to orthodox methods. I submit to the minister that times are not normal, and that this is not a time when we should consider the question of balancing the budget along orthodox and normal lines, because so far they have failed to permit of balancing it. However, let me deal with that later on.
Let me now turn to the third point, namely the protection of Canada's credit. Here again we have the minister dealing in superlatives:
If we continue this process of handing out unds without security-*
And I submit that was not a very fair statement of the case.
*-and without control of any sort, we shall be in danger of undermining dominion credit, which, in my opinion, must be protected at all costs.
I quite agree with the Minister of Finance that we must protect dominion credit. But when one takes that observation in conjunction with these other observations of what I call orthodox financial opinion of to-day it has a sinister meaning. We must protect the credit of Canada at all costs. If we are talking as patriotic Canadians-why, yes; everybody agrees. But if it means that we must protect the credit of Canada so as to ensure security to those who hold federal, provincial, municipal and corporate securities at high rates of interest, and maintain the sanctity, as they call it, of these contracts at their present level, then I do not agree with it.
One of the main criticisms by the orthodox group in 'this respect is the railway problem, or burden. Let me say a few things about it. I shall not sp.eak fully to-night, because I hope to have an opportunity to speak more fully in the course of the discussion of the bill now before tihe house concerning the railways. I do, however, wish to say a few words on this occasion. I submit "that unification means turning over the Canadian National Railways to a great transportation trust. In my opinion that is the plan which is behind all this agitation. So far as Canada is concerned, it is fascism in economics; that is what it is, and it will end in bondage of a more aggravated type than we have ever dreamed possible in Canada. I warn the house of the trend of affairs in that respect. I think the critics of the Canadian National Railways are grossly overstating .the case. The people are being terrified into a surrender of this
	. ...
valuable asset at less than cost; that is my firm conviction. If you tell a man daily he is ill, he will become ill. Years ago when I was a mischievous young fellow a few of us undertook to test this out. We met a certain man. and one after another told him that he was looking badly. In less than a week to my consternation he was in the hospital.
The point is that constant reiteration of a certain statement will fix in the public mind until it cannot be removed, a conviction which may not be true. In this instance I do not think it is true. We hear the statement that the Canadian National Railways problem is such that it is impossible for Canada to survive. I do not agree with that. Let us look at the matter for a minute. Out of the interest charges indicated in the budget about $SO,000,000 are directly due to the war; pensions and civil reestablishment account for $54,000,000 more. These two items add up to $134,000,000 of our present day budget. That sum has been accounted for during the last eighteen years; there has been no diminution and no asset is represented. When we talk about the country surviving and about the enormity of the problem presented by the Canadian National Railways, let us at least have some appreciation of other sections of the financial burden of Canada.
By the way, during the nine years hon. members opposite were in office, and while the succeeding government held office there has been no diminution of any amount in the debt. There was a slight drop for a few years, but it again increased. The point is that $134,000,000 of the minister's problem of $162,000,000 is due to the war, and, of course, we cannot avoid that; it is there and we have to face it. But why point to the Canadian National Railways, which in the last few years has had deficits of alarming dimensions, and say: This is what is going to ruin this country; this is what is going to destroy us? Well, Mr. Speaker, we have not been destroyed after eighteen years of paying $134,000,000 a year in interest and pensions on account of the war, for which expenditure we got nothing. That money all went up in smoke. But in the Canadian National Railways we have, as I said the other night, a magnificent plant. Do not let the people of this country be deluded into thinking they have nothing for the money which was put into the Canadian National Railways.
What is the suggestion of 'the government with regard to the railway problem? It is to substitute a board of directors for a board of trustees. That appeals to me as a sort of playing with tweedledum and bweedledee. It

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
does not make any very great difference which system of management you have except in this one case-and here I am going to say something very plain to the government- have they any serious grounds for this change? Is this action the fore-runner of a deliberate plan conceived by forces inside and outside this house to secure this great national asset at a mere fraction of its real value? Obviously the present proposals to deal with the problem of the Canadian National Railways are meaningless unless they are part of a deliberate plan hitherto undisclosed. And I think before the session closes there should be a full and complete disclosure to parliament of all the factors that lie behind this bill for the restoration of a directorate instead of a board of trustees for the Canadian National Railways.
I am told by those who know more about this question than I do that under the present statute under which the board of trustees was appointed it would be virtually impossible to bring about a scheme of amalgamation. But in the meantime the public mind is being poisoned. Apprehension, alarm, distortion of facts, despair of a solution, are being instilled. into the public mind, which already is harassed to the point of confusion and hopelessness by other troubles and discomforts. As I said a moment ago about the man who is driven sick by continually telling him that he is sick, by constantly instilling into the public mind the idea that our railway problem is hopeless, that we are faced with disaster; by arousing apprehension and alarm, you are going to create a condition of public mind which, I believe, some people hope will lead to the surrender of this asset at something less than its value. Let me ask this question: What, after all, are our real problems? I do not agree with the emphasis that tthe minister placed upon the problem. I would say that these are our two main problems: unemployment and debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is precisely what I myself said.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. The minister's only
reference to unemployment was a wave of the hand and a reference to the legislation before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh.no.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now I am going to ask this question: Can anything be done that has not been included in the budget? I think that is a fair question. Personally I think much can be done. The minister fears inflation, and the other day he certainly disclosed in a graphic way that he fears inflation. Of course, whenever the term "inflation" is used the suggestion
12739-X66i
is made that inflation of currency is meant such as Germany indulged in after the war. Usually that illustration is trotted out and it is said there is a long step between the inflation of the present government and what Germany did. I fear inflation of the kind that occurred in Germany just as much as the minister does, but what I fear more than inflation is deflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I fear them about equally.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I fear deflation more. That is just about the difference between us. After all, there are two degrees of inflation. There is inflation of currency, money, and there is inflation of credit. I am not going to discuss this question at length, but I will say briefly that between 19)25 and 1930 the bankers of the United States, and to a much lesser degree the bankers of Canada, indulged in an orgy of inflation of credit which, it is stated, resulted in a loss to the American people of something like one hundred billions of dollars. I think that is correct. But when you talk of Germany's inflation, there is no doubt that the inflation of credit which took place between 1925 and 1930 in the United States was equal in its effects almost to the inflation that took place in Germany. I see my time is passing and I must hasten on.
What has Britain done? I believe that wc can do much more than is proposed in the budget. Britain devalued the pound. It may be said that we followed, but we did not follow until after the United States, and the United States was about a year and a half after Britain. How well I remember, in the fall of 1931 and the spring of 1932, those who stood for sound money and all that sort of thing pointing to Britain as being the cause of a catastrophe to this country threatening the very life of the nation. I never agreed with them. It was not true, and we do not hear much about it to-day. Oh, no, it is a different story now. True, we have devalued the dollar, but we simply toddled along after Great Britain had given the lead, and after the Linked States had followed Britain's lead.
Britain has also adopted on a grand scale a housing scheme which has been discussed before in this house, and I mention it now to the minister only because we have hardly touched this question at all as compared with what Great Britain has done. The minister in his, speech about Britain referred to what we had done along similar lines, but he differs from the interpretation I put upon it the other night, so I shall not press that point. I simply say that in regard to housing we have not touched the question at all in the sense that Great Britain has.
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

Britain also took up industrial restoration on a wide scale. Let me read very briefly from the Midland Bank Review of July last, and this is worth listening to because, while what I say may not 'be of much importance, this is an authority. It reads:
It was perceived that the restrictive policy was having injurious effects on our economic life, and from time to time its strict eniorce-ment was modified in the interests of British industry and trade.
It goes on:
Stability of the value of the pound in terms of goods has replaced stability in terms of gold.
Do not let us forget that.
The essence of the matter is that Britain s monetary policy since 1931 has come to be formulated with first regard to the interests of British industry and trade.
That is what should be done in Canada, but it is not being done. Finance and banking are the servants of commerce and industry, and the sooner that truth is made cleat in our financial activities the better it will be for this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who says otherwise?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not the practice;
that is what I am referring to. Let me read another brief extract:
No lasting world recovery can be achieved, and no reconstruction of an international monetary system accomplished, until the complex and irregular web of international debts is cut away where necessary and brought *everywhere within the compass of the new structure of commodity prices.
That is what the Midland bank says. I shall not enlarge upon it; I submit it merely for what it is worth.
Before I pass on let tne say this: Since the deflation of the pound, through the leadership of the Bank of England-I am quoting now from the statement of the Bank of England-they have lowered the average yield on prime commercial paper, business undertakings' securities, from 5-7 per cent in early 1932 to 3*4 per cent. That does not include, as the statement shows, British government issues of any kind. It is a lowering of commercial rates, and that is what this country needs: a Lowering of commercial rates as well as of dominion rates.
What has Belgium done? In one year, Belgium has jumped from a condition of despair into a condition of almost complete release from depression. That was all done in one year, I repeat. A year ago last March she was in that condition; to-day her trade with the United Kingdom is up thirty-three per cent and unemployment has been reduced ,in the year twenty-six per cent.

Let me quote from Wigglesworth's, London, report of April of this year:
Fortunately there are rare examples of progress within the economic field, and Belgium provides an interesting lesson.
An article in the Sphere for 14th March gives a graphic account of the events in that country since the premier of Belgium, Mons. Van Zeeland, took office. On the eve of his retirement after twelve months of brilliantly successful ministry, it is profitable to record the marvellous progress made by this busy, highly industrialized little country of eight million inhabitants, which has blazed a trail for other countries whose financial and economic conditions continue unsatisfactory.... The banking system was the first to be reformed, and there can be no doubt that to this are due in no small part the credit facilities which contribute so much to the well-being of the country.
It goes on to show the result of the devaluation of the franc.
I quote now from the Midland bank review of April of this year:
To compare economic and financial conditions in Belgium to-day with those of a year ago is to observe a remarkable transformation, due mainly to the wisdom exercised in formulating and carrying out governmental policy in respect of business affairs. It is appropriate now to review the changes that have occurred, for the end of March concludes a chapter of economic reconstruction in a country which, through pressure of deflation, had been reduced to a condition of serious distress.
Power was taken to reduce its gold content by" not less than 25 and not more than 30 per cent On March 31 a new gold content was established at a figure 28 per cent below the old, and the exchange rates quickly adjusted themselves to the new level.
But listen to this:
The gold was revalued for the time being on the basis of the minimum prescribed reduction in the gold content of the currency, namely 25 per cent, and the immediate addition to the value of the gold holding, in terms of Belgian francs, was about 3,750 ^ millions. Leaving aside minor sums, 1,000 millions or rather more was allocated to each of three distinct purposes:	the establishment of an
exchange stabilization fund; the formation of a fund for steadying the market in government bonds; and the general purposes of the treasury, in particular, it is thought, the financing of public works.
This sum of 3,750 millions of francs would represent, roughly, $500,000,000.
That is what Belgium has done; she has taken definite steps, all within the ambit of present day law and possibility, but a departure from the orthodox method of financing. The statement is made in these reports that the result has been highly satisfactory:
One further consequence of devaluation needs to be mentioned: the great strengthening of the position of the National bank.
And so on. One might cite Sweden, Norway, Denmark, South Africa and other countries,

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
all of which have openly abandoned the tight money policy and adopted what is known as the easy money policy. The have used the credit of the nation to help agriculture and to restore industry and commerce. The question is: What can we do in this respect? As my time is rapidly passing, I should like to read twelve suggestions which I have to offer. I know perfectly well they will be misunderstood and misinterpreted by some, but I make these suggestions as an indication of what I think could be done in Canada without disturbing what is known as the general economic structure of the country. I am sorry to say to my hon. friends of the Canadian Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that I cannot follow them in their amendment owing to the last clause which refers to a capital levy and, I think, intimates more or less socialistic action.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member will come around in time.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that I shall come around in time. Well, I have studied it for a great many years, and while I appreciate their point of view and give them full credit for sincerity, I cannot follow them. But I do not think such action is necessary, for there is ample room for progressive, almost radical action without adopting such measures.
These are the suggestions I have to offer:
1.	Unreservedly determine not to increase our debt for three years-not even for deficits.
2.	Adopt a policy of refunding all existing dominion government bonds or dominion guaranteed bonds at a rate of interest below three per cent.
3.	On generous terms consolidate the dominion, provincial and certain municipal debts, providing such provinces or muncipialities as take advantage of the opportunity will undertake to make no new issues, the same as the dominion.
4.	Make the Bank of Canada in a true sense the government bankers, and utilize its powers of issue to the full extent, consistent with the principle of a twenty-five per cent coverage of gold for all outstanding notes.
5.	Use the system of issuing treasury bills as freely and as extensively as is done in Great Britain, having regard for difference in population.
6.	Utilize all surplus funds thus created for stabilization of exchange, purchase of outstanding bonds and general purposes of the government in relieving unemployment, et cetera.
7.	Retain in Canada a substantial proportion of our annual gold production for purposes indicated in the preceding paragraphs.
8.	Adopt a vigorous policy to encourage mining production by moderating taxation for a five year period and also by assisting smaller but proven properties into actual production.
9.	Relieve agriculture from the dominance of powerful quasi monopolies, especially in the live stock and dairy branch, and substitute friendly government cooperation for monopolistic private dictation. This can be done.
10.	Adopt a housing policy on a nationwide scale, along the lines of that in operation in Great Britain and Sweden.
11.	Provide useful and constructive employment by an extensive reforestation scheme and by elimination of level crossings-not in the petty way indicated in the estimates the other day.
12.	Let parliament declare for a just price to the farmer for his products and a fair wage to the worker; for it is only by the restoration of the purchasing power of these groups that commercial and industrial recovery can be achieved.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about silver?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, my views on silver are well known. I would put that in too.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But the hon, member left it out.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are many more suggestions I could put in, but what I am suggesting now are proposals capable of application without, I think, very much trouble. It, has been said of Thomas Jefferson, that great Democrat, that he failed when in office to put into practical operation the fine ideals he had preached when out of office. I think there is very much resemblance in that respect between the two great Democrats, the right hon,. leader of the government and Thomas Jefferson.
I will now quote from a publication which will be accepted, I think, by hon. members on the other side of the house and at my extreme right. I am sure that this extract, from the Canadian Liberal Monthly will be a fitting conclusion to my remarks:

Like many of those who have preceded me in this debate, I desire to extend to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) my congratulations upon his budget speech. His grasp of Canada's financial problems was commendable; his diction indeed was praiseworthy, and his delivery worthy of the highest praise which I can give him.
I regret that I cannot join with my horn, friend from Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who spoke this afternoon, in congratulating the Minister of Finance upon the tariff provisions of his budget. I listened with a good 
deal of pleasure and considerable profit, as I usually do, to the address of my (hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar, but when he was dealing with the reduction in the tariff upon agricultural implements I could not help thinking that he and I approached the problem from different viewpoints. He approached it from the viewpoint of the agriculturist, and his main desire apparently was to procure for agriculturists cheap agricultural implements. I approach the problem from the standpoint of the worker in industry, the people whom I represent, and I am free to confess that my concern is: Will it create jobs or will it not create jobs?
Yet, Mr. Speaker, I could not help feeling that probably the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and I would not be far apart in trying to arrive at some solution of our problem if only we had before us the facts relative ito the situation. I am not one of those who have been of opinion that tariffs should be, as some one expressed it in this house the other day, as high as Haman's gallows. I am one of those who have always believed that we should have protective tariffs, and I am inclined to the view that my friend from Rosetown-Biggar would not disagree with that principle so long as he was satisfied that, included in that measure of protection, there was not a return upon watered stock and what was not true capital. But in connection with the provision in this budget for agricultural implements, we had no opportunity to ascertain what was the correct and fair rate to provide protection in that industry, protection to provide jobs for those in whom I am particularly interested, and to provide reasonable prices to those agricultural consumers in whom my hon. friend is primarily interested. Here we had a case where an investigation was pending that would have given us all those facts which we should have. In the midst of it, for some reason best known to the government, there is this drastic reduction made in the protective tariff applicable to the agricultural implement industry. I suggest to my 'hon. friend the Minister of Finance that, as undoubtedly he will be replying in closing this budget debate, in doing so he give me some reason to believe that the action of the government in taking this step in the midst of the inquiry was other than .to pacify an insistent demand from some of his agricultural representatives and supporters in the House of Commons from western Canada who wanted a cut in the tariff on agricultural implements, no matter What might be the result to industry or to the job-hunters of this country.

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
I could almost believe, as I heard the budget, that my hon. friend had adopted some of the psychology which was being advocated by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) to-night, except that I think the minister probably proceeded according to that system which is known as Coueism, and instead of dealing in his budget with the major problems of Canada, he proceeded to say: Every day in every way things are getting better and better.

They, the people of this country, were not prepared to go the length of voting for what to them were such radical ideas as those advocated by my social credit friends or those advocated by my Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends, but they were in favour of a change and so the vast majority of them voted for the Liberal party. speechtext:
we shall witness some reduction in the value of the dollar. There will be two alternatives to consider: on the one hand, a new devaluation, on the other, an inflation with the maintenance of the present gold parity.
Again:
If a country cannot bring its budget into real equilibrium, it cannot in the long run withstand an inflation of the currency, no matter what means are tried.
My final quotation is this:
An inflation in America could not fail to affect the currency position in England.
And, of course, by inference in Canada.
In that country too everything is prepared for a price advance. The country is well provided with means of payment, which could be better utilized than is the case at present. The official financial policy, as formulated at the London conference and in the program of the sterling bloc, aims at a moderate price advance, which must be considered desirable also from the point of view of the combating of unemployment. If such a rise of prices could be attained in harmony with the trend of development in the United States, this would no doubt be viewed with favour in England. The conditions in Sweden are similar, and indeed the sterling bloc in general would gladly join in a moderate price advance promoted by England and the United States jointly.
So that the whole situation is that we are face to face with conditions in our financial system which may change overnight, and there is no evidence, none at all in the construction of the budget or in the inferences to be developed from a study of it, that these matters are in the mind of the government.
Again, the hon. Minister of Finance, while regretting the fact, is still content to accept the burden of interest so that thirty-six per cent of the country's revenue is to be earmarked to that contribution. As I have already said, the distressing claim of interest which, like a canker, eats into every part of the body politic, is in every business, every home, every activity of our lives and must be eradicated. I cited Ruskin a few days ago. Can anyone cast a stone at him? Can anyone cast his efforts aside in preference to those of, say the much quoted Carlyle? Ruskin became conscious of the curse of interest and realizing his assets, he eschewed all interest on his investments and spent

capital sums. Thirty-six per cent of our country's revenue absorbed in interest! It is there that the axe must be laid at the root of the tree, and I propose to point this out again and again, for the fact is that interest must go. As I have already said, our personal and social activities will fail where-ever in any particular they transgress the laws of nature or, as some say, - the laws of God. The squirrel does not get interest on the nuts he stores in the hollows of the tree. The camel does not get interest on the fat he stores in his hump or in the water he stores in the cells of his stomach lining. The butter-tailed sheep does not get interest on the fat it stores in its tail. I can discover nothing to justify humanity in prostrating itself before the Juggernaut of interest, that Juggernaut which humanity itself has so laboriously constructed. Interest must go.
Again, I see very little sympathy between the recent trade agreement with the United States and this budget; they do not conform. They have been constructed by minds which have very little in common, for otherwise the minister would stand absolutely condemned for giving with one hand and taking away with the other. I consider the increase in the sales tax an oppression of the poor of the country. I notice in the newspapers that the leading merchants of Ottawa and district, speaking last Saturday of the budget and this sales tax in particular, said that it would not bother them; that they could take it in their stride and still preserve the status quo. If that is correct, it shows a situation that needs investigation, but I cannot think it is true. I am satisfied that the raising of money by this increase in the sales tax is an added burden on the wage earners of Canada. But more important than all else is the awful burden of debt. Year after year big business escapes its just share of taxation. By one plea after another, by one threat after another those who have encourage the government to take from those who have not. The freedom of the big business man from his relative share of the public obligations has continued so long as to develop a condition of immunity which has been very strongly reflected in this budget. There is not a plutocrat in the country who can quarrel with the Minister of Finance in his sublime capitalist effort. But that will not bring prosperity to Canada; it will not reduce our national debt. That can come only by the government inserting itself between the big business man and the successful gouges by which he achieves his wealth. It will come only by a forthright effort to compel the abundantly wealthy to

The Budget-Miss Macphail
tighten the traces when pulling this country out of the slough of despond in which we find it.
A plea was made earlier in the session for pensions for the blind of the dominion. This plea was refused on grounds of budget necessity, but in view of the acceptance of a probable loss in budgeting of 3100,000,000, I am still quite unable to see why the blind should not be permitted to realize some satisfaction entering into their lives even during this session. Apart from all these large issues I cannot sit down without drawing attention to the plight of the small fruit and vegetable farmers all over the country already labouring under the physical disadvantages of a colder climate than that of their competitors to the south. They are having the salt rubbed into their wounds with no possible signs of relief.
I commend that thought to the Minister of Finance.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce): In beginning I sincerely wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon his budget address delivered on the first of May. It. was a pleasing address, interesting in its content and construction, in the beauty and simplicity of its language, and in its forceful and agreeable delivery. Though it lasted two and a half hours the Minister of Finance held the attention of the whole house for that long time. He must have found it an exhausting task, but it was certainly one which was exceedingly well performed.
I find that all budgets are alike in this, that each contains some things which one likes and some things which one does not like. If you vote for a budget you are voting for some things with which you do not agree, and if you vote against it you are voting against some things with which you do agree. It seems impossible, therefore, to avoid that dilemma. I felt that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well) expressed my thought almost perfectly this afternoon and there is no use in going over it again in detail. There were in the budget things which anyone representing an agricultural constituency would be pleased with, but I could not be pleased over the eight per cent sales tax. I am opposed to the sales tax because it taxes most heavily those who spend their entire income on consumptive goods, while those who spend only a very small portion of their income on such goods pay a relatively small sales tax.
Then, too, I am unorthodox in the matter of balancing budgets. In times when individuals cannot borrow and when individuals cannot spend, governments must
borrow and governments must spend. I do not say that governments ought to borrow, but under the present financial system they must and they do. The balancing of the budget is not by any means as important as it is generally thought to be, because the payment of sums of money without which it will not balance, would undoubtedly in practice divert large sums of money into already bulging pockets. For, as I said a moment ago, there are people, many of them bondholders, who do not spend their incomes in order to live; and since, as has been stated in this house, I believe, thousands of times, a loan creates a deposit and the repayment of a loan destroys a deposit, the balancing of the budget might conceivably destroy a portion at any rate and possibly a large portion of the $162,000,000 by which the budget does not balance. In other words, it would, as the Minister of Finance admitted, tend to cause severe deflation. I believe there are a great many people both in the house and outside who still think that governments should act like individuals and should not spend, particularly in a time of depression.
I hold the other view, that in times of depression governments should spend, in order to make up the amount which individuals cannot spend; and in good times, when individuals can spend, governments should curtail their expenditures.
We have heard a lot, particularly in this debate, about the need of a change in the financial system. I enjoyed very much this evening the speech made by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens). I have enjoyed, too, other speeches during this debate which have related to money. A large number of Canadians-not yet a majority, but an increasing number-believe that a change in the financial system is necessary; that we shall come to base our credit and currency upon real wealth; that it will be issued in the first place by a federal authority

possibly the Bank of Canada when it becomes a government bank-without interest, and that we shall benefit largely from it in one way or another. I suggest that one method of using a government issue of money, which could well be considered under such a system, would be the cutting of farm mortgages in two and reimbursing the creditors by the issue of noninterest bearing bonds.
Since the Liberals came into power with such a very large majority, there has been a tendency rather to scoff at monetary reform. If a certain newspaper story is to be believed, pressure is being brought to bear upon two Liberal members who have done great service
The Budget-Miss Macphail

to the party and to the country by the speeches they have made this session in the house. That, during the campaign, other Liberals talked similarly, this little pamphlet shows. It was issued by the Parkdale Liberal Association during the campaign, and it is really a very intelligent production. It states:
At present the privately owned banking system of Canada has the exclusive right to manufacture money (bank credit and currency are both money).
The Liberal party proposes to take this exclusive right away from the banking system and give it to the federal government.
And then the candidate goes on to say:
I agree with the Hon. J. L. Ralston, who says that he does not favour universal public ownership, but that the control of currency and credit is properly a public utility and should be operated as such.
I feel that I must take time to put on Hansard one or two other paragraphs:
The banking system manufactures "money" just as definitely as Massey-Harris manufacture ploughs.
Apparently that is not going to be very definitely.
But they do not "sell" this money-(and they certainly do not give it away)-but what they really do is to rent it and they call the rent "interest."
It goes on:
Now, if the government can authorize private banks to create money, why can the government not create money itself?
For a long time I have been looking for an answer to that question. Then the pamphlet
says:
This is what the Rt. Hon. Mackenzie King means when he says:-
"Usury once in control will wreck any nation. Until the control of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and most sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile."
That is very good. At the bottom of the next page they say, in red letters:
What Difference?
The difference between banker and national control of the creation of money is briefly this:-Under banker control the bank creates money and rents it to the government. Under government control the government creates its own money and pays rent to nobody.
Then- the names of certain people are given.
I quote:
In a pamphlet this size one can only scratch the surface of this all-important, all-embracing subject. There is no other subject of such vital importance to the happiness and wellbeing of 95 per cent of the Canadian people. It is being stressed by an imposing list of people, among whom I mention-
Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King.

speechtext:
