To proceed, there never was a time when agriculture needed organization more than it does now, and unfortunately the industry is poorly organized at this time. In order to do anything effective towards basing the selling price of farm products upon the cost of production there will have to be one hundred per cent organization of agriculture and there will have to be export and import boards; in other words pretty definite planning of agricultural production and sale, will be necessary and we are coming closer to this all the time.
Before closing, I should like to suggest one other point that, I think, would help agriculture. It is that a good deal of the loss to agriculturists, as is well known to every member of the house, takes place somewhere between the time the goods leave their farms and the time they arrive at the tables of the consumers. Not only is that true; the increased cost to the consumer takes place in the same interval. It will not be so very long before we shall be driven to the construction of cooperative processing plants on a very large scale, with government assistance and direction, or government controlled or owned processing plants, because until agriculture is again able to purchase the goods that are being turned out so rapidly by the machines and until the unemployed and the low paid workers are able to purchase goods there will be no revival of prosperity in Canada. There may be spasmodic upward turns, but they will not last until the mass of the people of Canada are free to use the products and the services which they themselves produce.
Mr. LOUIS P. A. ROBICHAUD (Kent, NB.):	Mr. Speaker, may I crave the indulgence of the house in the few observations that I am about to make in the language better understood by the majority of hon. members. I confess that I do so with some degree of apprehension, inasmuch as I have ventured to make this maiden speech in a tongue not my own. I take the opportunity at the outset sincerely to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon his able and brilliant expose of the budget. He has done honour not only to himself but to this house and to the country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to give some of the impressions of a new member since coming to this house in February. Adverting first to the speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on

the address, since "a tout seigneur tout hon-neur," may I be allowed to say, with all deference and respect, that despite the no small admiration aroused in me by his great ability, his masterly handling of the English language, and his brilliancy of delivery, I have not as yet been able to shake off the impression I received at the time that the speech was what I would call a "Bourbon" speech.
Coming to the speech of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), may I be allowed to congratulate the hon. member most sincerely upon having, after "walking so long in the valley of the shadow of darkness," at long last seen the light. I like to believe in the sincerity of the hon. member's conversion, but if I may be permitted to say so, instead of leaving the fold and venturing abroad to evangelize and convert the Gentiles, would it not have been the better thing to do for him to remain in the "shepberdy" and with his splendid eloquence and great powers of conviction to apply himself to the role of the leaven to leaven the whole inert mass of his party?
Coming next to the speeches of hon. members of the extreme left, I say I am in accord with many of the sentiments they expressed. We all realize that the world this last five years has been passing through a period of travail, misery and pain. But, may I ask, was there ever anything worth while came to this world except through travail, misery and pain? Mr. Speaker, I believe that an evolution, though, perhaps imperceptible, has been operating not only for the last five years but for the last ten, yes, the last fifteen years, and that the world is gradually shaping for and moving towards a rebirth. But let me warn my hon. friends of the extreme left to be careful not to apply the injection used in such cases prematurely lest it bring about a miscarriage.
I am convinced that the heart of every hon. member is in the right place and goes out to poor suffering humanity. Indeed, I believe it is the same old heart wherever man may be found on the face of the earth, and has been the same in all ages, the same old heart that pulsated in the very breast of the father of mankind; with this difference, however, that to-day man has a more profound knowledge of its intense longings and aspirations. The secret of life as I see it is to acquire a better understanding of such longings and aspirations. Indeed, was it not Socrates who set before man as the highest attainment of human wisdom, to know oneself, in other words, to know in all their intricacies the workings of the human heart?

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud
Here, sir, may I compare the old human heart to a finely cut diamond with innumerable facets and angles, slowly revolving upon itself, and that revolving movement accelerated by the passing of generations and the advent of new civilizations, and may I suggest that with the advent of Christianity a powerful impulse was imparted whereby the full revolution was completed at one stroke?
It is sometimes said that the trouble to-day is that man is living in a new world, but so far has been unable to adapt himself to his new world. But I have a different philosophy. The trouble, sir, is that alter a struggle of nineteen centuries' duration man has not yet been able to conquer that world and its ways, and attune it to the vibrating radiations of those new facets and angles of the human heart uncovered by the advent of Christianity. To illustrate: I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that at one time or another you have come into contact with some of those men described in this very house, I believe, as gangsters of high finance. Tell me, sir, as man to man, did you find them very much different from yourself? Yet the moment they enter into their councils of deliberation we are asked to believe that they lose all humane feelings. It is a sad reflection, but can it be that they partake of the nature of the wolf, the lone wolf being very timid and harmless, while the pack wolf is terribly daring and cruel? If that be so, there you have it: the ways of the world versus the human heart.
It has been said in this house that politics is a science. I am not in futl agreement with that view. To my mind politics is more an art than a science. It has to do with the heart rather than the head. In this connection I am reminded of an ex-Prime Minister of this country-he is not now a member of this house-to whom I once listened with great intellectual delight. He certainly was and is an intellectual giant, and one could not help being fairly amazed at his power and keenness of mind. He could split a hair in four and pursue the four splits to their bitter ends. But as a politician and a leader of men he was not a success. To be a successful leader of men one has to keep a fairly even balance between head and heart. Let the heart give in too much to the head and we have the type of government with which my hon. friends to my immediate left have afflicted the country in the immediate past. On the other hand let the head give way unduly to the heart and we would have the kind of government that would afflict this country should my hon. friends on our extreme left take the reins of power. So I say with Bobby Burns:
The heart ay's the part ay
That makes us right or wrong.
One often hears it said that the government should be run on business lines; that there should be more business men in the house instead of lawyers, doctors and so forth. Well all I have to say to that is, that badly as the political business of the country has been managed in the past, the good Lord help the country had it been as badly managed, or rather mismanaged, as industrial and financial business has been. We hear on every side how highly developed and efficiently organized industry is to-day. If that is meant to apply to the individual units of industry, I concede. But I feel that industry considered as a whole and as a single entity has not yet learned to walk. That is a strong statement.
We have heard it said in the house that there is many an industry which should never have been established in Canada because it was economically unsound. But on account of vested interests thus created the question was asked: What can we do about it now? What I am concerned with is this: What are we doing to prevent a repetition of the same course of events in the future? Apparently we are doing nothing. But remember, Mr. Speaker, I am not placing the responsibility on parliament; I am placing it where it belongs, on industry itself, for I believe that the greatest incentive to progress is not so much profit and greed as it is vesting people with responsibility and developing in them a due sense of that responsibility. And so I believe the time has arrived for industry to provide itself with a general staff-call it "The national council of industry," or whatever suitable name you wish to give it-and proceed on really scientific lines. It would be the business of that general staff to keep industry informed as to the needs and requirements of their own people and the people of foreign countries, and to keep a sharp eye on racketeers of high and low finance. It would be the business of that general staff to see that no investment is directed to the building up of a unit of industry economically unsound, or to the overbuilding in any given line such as has been done in the paper industry in Canada, or the textile industry of the United States.
In this connection I am reminded of a mission of English business men who two or three years ago made an investigation of the American and Japanese textile industry. What did they report? They reported that the social condition of textile employees in Japan was just about on a par with that of American and English employees, but that with her
9,000,000 spindles Japan produced as much as the United States did with their 31,000,000 spindles. I leave hon. members to draw all

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud

the inescapable conclusions. May I add that thought would have to be given to the advisability or otherwise of giving representation on that council of industry to the other partners interested, namely labour and the consumers.
I am not a prophet, nor indeed the son of a prophet, but may I venture to make a few predictions which I believe, will see their fulfilment in the not far distant future.
First, I see the day when each and every nation will confine itself to converting its own raw materials only into the finished product.
Second, I see the day when the proletarian army will have acquired a much greater mobility than it has to-day and so, like a nilitary army in the field, it will be directable .0 any needed point on short notice. In view >f that I have my doubts as to the wisdom of encouraging members of that army to build and own their own homes. I believe industry should build the homes needed by that army. They could build on a large scale and much more economically than the individuals themselves, to whom such homes would be let at a cost rental.
Third, and as a consequence of predictions numbers one and two, I foresee the day- I may not see it myself, but verily I believe my children will see it-when we shall have free trade throughout the .world, preceded of course by an evolutionary stage when geographical economic units will constitute themselves along the line of the dream of the late Aristide Briand for the European nations, and of the fact of the forty-eight states to the south of us.
In the nature of things, this is bound to come about. Does it stand to reason that nations should spend millions and billions of dollars in removing natural obstacles from the channels of trade, and the next moment erect artificial obstacles by way of tariff walls. In this connection it is a consolation to think that the insane frenzy of economic nationalism from which the world is just emerging will have been the most potent factor in bringing about this final desired result.
Fourth, I foresee the day when the net surplus exports of a nation will be paid for directly by the people of that very nation, and be considered as an extension of their own domestic market, instead of the indirect way in which those exports are now paid for, namely by the exporting nation investing the pro'ceeds of that surplus in the country of importation. To-day that is the only way. in which such surplus exportation can be paid for, since there is no gold to pay for them and the said exporting nation will not accept

any more goods in return. They simply invest the proceeds of the surplus in the country of importation.
Now, as to the remedies, in addition to the ones already suggested. People will say that what we need is inflation or deflation. We have had considerable of that in the various nations of the world since the fatidic year of 1929, but the inflation and deflation which I have in mind are of another sort. They are not so much a monetary inflation and deflation as an inflation of hearts and a deflation of heads.
Again I could say with the Tiger of France, Clemenceau, who at one time could hardly be accused of being a Christian, "If every Christian was a Christian in fact as well as in name, there would no longer be any social question." But that might sound too much like a sermon. So I would prescribe as the proper tonic for our patient, the world, preparatory to the many operations he will have to undergo, just a little more inflation of hearts and a little more deflation of heads.
I am convinced that, I will not say the doctrine, or even the principles of Liberalism, but simply Liberal and democratic philosophy or Liberal and democratic state of mind will provide the best cure for the economic ills of the world. It has been said in the house by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) that because of its history and its ancient principles the Liberal party had an opportunity unsurpassed in scope. May I say that there are no ancient principles of the Liberal party. The principles of that party are ever young and living, constantly rejuvenated to suit the times and always abreast in the march of time.
Mr. Speaker, I trust I have not bored you unduly with these vagaries of mine, and in conclusion may I express my deep appreciation to my colleagues and to you for the kindly forbearance and considerate attention which they and you have accorded me.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our industrial, financial and political leaders assured the people year after year during the depression that we were on our way to better and happier days; that prosperity was- just around the comer. At the same time the policy - of wage cutting, "tighten your belt," and other policies of economy were introduced, All this has led to a great shrinkage in purchasing power. Prices to farmers for their products fell below the cost of production; credit -was withdrawn by financial institutions, and this great reduction to the farmers because of

The Budget-Mr. Landeryou
this decline in the prices of their products has been estimated by Premier Bracken of Manitoba at approximately one billion dollars for a period of four years. This great shrinkage in purchasing power has led to a reduction or restriction in consumption, which in turn has been reflected in the slowing up of factories, adding to the number of the unemployed, and thereby increasing the difficulties of municipal, provincial and federal governments in their financing. It has also increased the burdens upon our taxpayers, If we are going to solve this problem we must restore to the people this lost purchasing power.
The years of the depression have caused the people of this country to make a thorough analysis of our economic system. They are becoming convinced that this policy of "tighten your belt," economize, produce below the cost of production, will not solve the problem. Apparently they realize to-day better than ever before, especially those many millions who gaze at the various articles on display in our so-called stores-I refer to them many times as museums-where people go to see the things they would like to buy if they only had the money, or who look at the catalogues sent to them by the great merchandising corporations in this country, gazing at them as they would at the family album, seeing there the things they would like to buy if they only had the money- the great masses of our people, I repeat, realize to-day better than ever before that they must have restored to them the purchasing power necessary to bring back prosperity. This can be done, I believe, by the use and control of national credit by the government, that national credit to be used in the interest of the people to meet the needs of the people. We hear a great deal these days about sound money. What the people of Canada want is more money and less sound. The farmers want more purchasing power for their production, the worker more for his labour, the fisherman more for his fish, and industry in general requires more for new and greater developments.
We in this part of the house are in favour of sound money; we want sound money. We are not-inflationists; we are not deflationists. However we do not believe that money to be sound must be based upon the intrinsic value of gold or silver. We believe that money should be based upon our collective ability to produce real wealth and render service one to. another, and that it should actually-reflect any increase in our ability-to 12739-167$
do so. Our wealth should not be measured only in dollars and cents; it should be measured in our volume of goods that are being or can be produced. The link between production and distribution is money or purchasing power, and we must restore purchasing power to the people to do away with these stored up surpluses that we have in the midst of this distress and suffering.
We have another problem, and that is the problem of debt. This problem of debt must be faced. To-day our money and our credit have been used as an instrument to create debt. By the creation of these enormous interest bearing debts this instrument has been used for the purpose of destruction, and we should bend our efforts to the reduction of private and public interest bearing debts. We do not say, repudiate, nor do we say, default, but if the creditor in this country is going to insist upon the pound of flesh from a debtor already reduced to skin and bone there will be left nothing but a skeleton, of little use to the creditor, the debtor himself or his country.
To-day the banks pay lower rates of interest to depositors. The enormous sum of $600,000,000 has been dropped in one year by holders of life insurance policies. Then we have a decline in revenue from real estate properties. I have in mind the memory of those 600,000 men who went overseas prepared to give their lives in a period of national crisis, and now the question is being asked of those who hold the bonds: Just what sacrifice are you prepared to make at this time of national crisis? The people of Canada are awaiting the answer. They insist upon cooperation. I do not blame the municipal or provincial governments to-day who. faced with bankruptcy, faced with the choice of needs of their people or meeting these interest bearing charges, insist upon refunding their obligations at lower rates of interest. Rather I would place the blame or responsibility, if there is any blame or responsibility to be placed, upon the governments that preceded them and borrowed these huge sums of money and spent them as they have done; They are the ones to blame, if there is any blame to be put upon anyone. .
From time to time people point with pride to the. fact that we have sound money and safe banking institutions. Is it necessary that all classes of society should sustain great losses; that 1,200,000 people should remain on relief; that the farmers of Canada should, produce wealth below cost- of production? Must people lose their , homes and must the conditions of distress now profiling in .the
The Budget-Mr. Landeryou

country continue in order that we may be able to point with pride to the fact that our banks are safe? I believe our banking institutions can remain safe and our money sound and still allow us to solve the problem that faces us. The solution lies in the proper use of the national credit. Many people contend that favourable balanoes of trade will bring prosperity. The United States has enjoyed1 favourable trade balances for many years; in fact it is estimated that all told they amount to over $27,000,000,000. Can we truthfully say that the United States is enjoying prosperity? The answer is no. Canada, for the last five years, has enjoyed favourable trade balances, and yet at the same time, as has been pointed out, unemployment has increased. The problem in Canada is to provide out of our natural resources sufficient to saturate the domestic market, creating at the same time a surplus which could be used to exchange those things not naturally produced in Canada, possibly on a quid pro quo basis or goods for goods.
The question has been asked of us in this house: Just what do you mean by control of credit? We do not believe that the purchase of a controlling interest in the central bank is a solution. Changing the ownership of the monetary system will not solve the problem but changing the policy will do something towards bringing about a solution. We believe that credit should be controlled by the three principles advocated by social credit, namely: a just price which will guarantee to labour a just wage for its contribution; a just price to the farmer and all others who provide the raw materials necessary for the production of wealth, and a fair commission to those who own or supervise our industries. We believe also in the continuous flow of credit, which means the circulation of money or purchasing power that can be assured by various methods, especially by the payment of a national dividend to all citizens of the country, assuring them economic security and providing for them at least the bare necessities of life. This would encourage the spending of money and do away with the fear which seems to grip the consumer to-day. Many people neglect to buy to-day the things they need because of fear of economic insecurity which may overtake them to-morrow. The people of Canada want economic security. They do hot want the feasts or the famines of the past created by a monetary system, possibly I should say by the uncontrolled, unsupervised manipulation of the monetary system by private individuals, which eminent economists and statesmen declare will chill, check and destroy genuine economic freedom. This

question of money has been brought up in the house many times, but apparently the government is not yet prepared to introduce any monetary reforms; at any rate the budget does not disclose any such intention. They still imagine that we can tax our way to prosperity or borrow ourselves out of debt.
We have been referred to as radicals, as leftists, but I contend that we have a' sane solution to offer to the people, and I am looking forward to the day when a social credit minister of finance will bring down a budget which will indicate a solution of the many problems that confront the country today, problems which some of our leading statesmen declare will bring ruin and disaster to Canada. We see no ruin and disaster to the credit of this country if we will but make use of our national credit. We do not fear the collapse of financial credit as long as the real credit of the country remains intact. As long as we have our great railways running; aa long as there are men on the farms; as long as the laws of nature are favourable to the production of goods which we need; as long as we have all the real wealth in the country and the ability to produce, we need not fear anything. The collapse of financial credit is, therefore, not of much concern to us. We say that that which is physically possible will be financially possible under a just monetary system.
Mr. H. E. WILTON (Hamilton West); I wish to congratulate the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Landeryou) upon his ideas of old age; I am glad to know he feels that he is going to live to be a very old man. In passing, I noticed in to-day's morning papers that the hon. and might I add charming, lady members of this house can divert their minds from the serious business of unemployment, added taxation and budget overdrafts to tihe more pleasing study of masculine defects due to lop ears, crooked noses and avoirdupois. Perhaps this interesting analysis of our physical defects may have the subduing effect of shorter speeches and thereby prove of great value in solving the perplexing financial problems which confront us. Perhaps when the members for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) and the Yukon (Mrs. Black) next have their teacups read, a Prince Charming will be revealed. Let us hope for the best.
As an individual member, representing an individual but outstanding constituency, I realize my duty to that constituency, but I also realize my duty in a broader sense to every citizen of Canada, particularly to that important majority known as "the taxpayer:"

The Budget-Mr. Wilton
The outstanding feature of the revised tariff act, according to its supporters, is that it will increase the buying power of the Canadian dollar. Last Saturday, while I was in Hamilton, a hardware merchant of that city showed me a certain article on sale in his store retailing at ten cents. He told me that this article was manufactured in the city of Hamilton and that he purchased it at forty-five cents per dozen. Quite recently representatives of Japanese firms had called upon him and offered him this same article at thirty cents per dozen. The point is this, as he said, "Although I may and probably will buy those Japanese goods at thirty cents per dozen, as against the forty-five cents per dozen asked here, I shall not sell them at less than the price I am selling them at now, so that the only person who will benefit by that will be the retail dealer and not the man who buys to use."
Hamilton, because of its hundreds of large manufacturing concerns, is known far and near as the Pittsburgh of Canada. What will this new reduced tariff act do to that great city? It will decrease employment; it has done so already, and it will increase public relief, which in turn will increase taxation to the already overburdened taxpaying homeowner. Of what use is increased buying power to the man out of work and without money? The reduced tariff on automobiles would imply reduced cost to Canadians, but such is not the case, because the increase in sales tax more than offsets the tariff reduction. Last week I was told by a representative salesman of a large automobile sales concern in Hamilton that the agents of that company had been called in to their head office last Saturday morning and instructed to add $18 to the price of every car they offered for sale. I said to him, "Your cars should sell cheaper, due to the reduction in tariff," and the answer was "They should, had it not been for the sales tax, which more than offsets the reduction in tariff and adds $18 to the price of our car." This is a low priced car.
There is an old saying that nothing is so bad but it might be worse. So, perhaps we should be thankful that the situation is no worse than it is. I do not agree with those who say that we have passedi through the worst depression the world has ever known. Ancient history belies the statement. A hundred years ago, yes, and two hundred years ago, the same cry was being made, as is indicated by an extract I have in my hand, taken from the writings of Lord Macaulay Writing in 1830, he speaks of conditions over
a century ago, and also makes reference in this essay to a period one hundred years prior to that time:
The present moment is one of great distress. But how small will that distress appear when we think over the history of the last forty years; a war, compared with which all others sink into insignificance; taxation, such as the most heavily taxed people of former times could not have conceived; a debt larger than all the public debts that ever existed in the world added together; the food of the people studiously rendered dear; the currency imprudently debased, and and imprudently restored. Yet is the country poorer than in 1790? We firmly believe that in spite of all the misgov-ernment of her rulers-
They were complaining about misgovemment then.
-she has been almost constantly becoming richer and richer. Now and then there has been a stoppage, now and then a short retrogression; but as to the general tendency there can be no doubt. A single breaker may recede but the tide is evidently coming in.
If we were to prophesy that in the year 1930 a population of fifty millions, better fed, clad, and lodged than the English of our time, will cover these islands-that machines constructed on principles yet undiscovered will be in every house-that our debt vast as it seems to us, will appear trifling to our great-grand-children, many people would think us insane. We prophesy nothing; but this we say: If any person had told the parliament which met after the crash of 1720 that in 1830 the wealth of England would surpass their wildest dreams-stage-coaches would run frpm London to York in twenty-four hours, that men would be in the habit of sailing without wind, and would be beginning to ride without horses, our ancestors would have given as much credit to the prediction as they gave to "Gulliver's Travels."__
We cannot absolutely prove that those are in error who tell us that society has reached a turning point, that we have seen our best days. But so said all who came before us, and with just as much apparent reason.
So, after all, we find that two hundred years ago, and again one hundred years ago, the same cry we hear to-day was in evidence. Perhaps we may be glad that conditions are no worse than they are. Regardless of tariffs, budgets, polities and pessimists, the great problem of unemployment, public relief and a rapidly increasing national debt will never be solved by the vicious system of borrowing money with which to pay debts. Borrowed money never paid a debt. It simply adds to the 'burden, and finally finds its way to the tax bill of the homeowner. We reduce national income by reducing tariffs, and adjust the financial loss by increased taxation. This tariff act in its present form will divert Canadian manufacturing concerns to the United States, and put Canadians out of work. The only solution is new, additional sources
Criminal Code

of revenue, which I think I referred to a few days ago, other than by direct taxation. If I had in my garden a good crop of potatoes, it would be most ridiculous for me to borrow from my neighbour money with which to go out and purchase potatoes. It would be no more ridiculous, however, than what our governments are doing. With our na-;ional back yard filled with gold, silver and valuable minerals of various kinds, we go out and borrow money, leaving our rich mineral deposits in the hands of private concerns to exploit and profit by, while we as a government continue to sink deeper in the mire of borrowed money debts. So long as we continue this kind of thing, this vicious circle of borrowing money with which to pay borrowed money, we shall have no good reason to complain if the lady members of this house refer to us, not only as lop-eared, but as irresponsible incompetents.

On motion of Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East) the house adjourned at 1053 p.m.
